newsitem.title: MOROCCO: FEATURE - Algeria to elect parliament in polls excluding radicals.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Algeria to elect parliament in polls excluding radicals.

text.p: Algeria votes in 1997 for its first parliament for five years after redrawing the political map to exclude Moslem radicals.

But analysts see no letup in the violence in which about 60,000 people have died, including more than 200 civilians since November, and which started after the authorities scrapped elections Islamic fundamentalists were set to win.
Almost all agree that security has improved in the past year, especially in cities. "But it is very difficult to eliminate," one senior Western diplomat said of the violence.

Pointing to recent mass killing of villagers in mountainous areas south of Algiers, he said the "horrible method of killing them" -- most had their throats slit -- is "a sign of the fact they (the rebels) are lacking weapons."
Algeria's 29 million people have had no parliament since January 1992 when then president Chadli Benjedid announced he had dissolved it days earlier, and that he was resigning.
Diplomats said he was ousted by the military and officials because he was willing to accept an Islamist-dominated assembly after his reforms ended the era of a single ruling party.

President Liamine Zeroual, who won legitimacy in a presidential election in 1995 and backing to change the constitution last month, has redrawn the political map ahead of the parliamentary elections planned for the first half of 1997.
This could lead to more stability, analysts said.

The London-based Control Risks organisation said in its outlook for 1997: "Zeroual's project is setting the country on the road to political stabilisation, though the long-term outlook remains highly uncertain.
"The potential rewards could outweigh the risks for foreign investors -- as long as comprehensive security procedures are ensured for all personnel and premises."
TALKS WITH FIS FAILED

One foreign economic analyst, who asked not to be named, said: "The 'terrorists' can't win. The situation has changed from the days of the FIS (Islamic Salvation Front) as a legal party with popular support."
Zeroual tried to negotiate with jailed leaders of the FIS. Talks failed and he has now effectively eliminated the movement, outlawed in 1992, as a political force, say diplomats.
Under a new constitution, approved by referendum, parties based on religion, language or region are banned.
A new electoral law also threatens two strong regional parties -- war veteran Hocine Ait Ahmed's Socialist Forces Front (FFS) and Said Saadi's Rally for Culture and Democracy (RCD).

One Western diplomat speaking from Algiers saw vast changes for what he called "the gamble of the elections", with the legal moderate Islamist party, Hamas, strong against the RCD and the FFS, which came second to the FIS in December 1991.

"Hamas is the party which has best infiltrated society. It is everywhere in the country," he said, adding it would do everything necessary to meet new party laws. Hamas leader Sheikh Mahfoud Nahnah came second to Zeroual with more than a quarter of the votes in the presidential poll.
The National Liberation Front (FLN) which ran Algeria for nearly 30 years has its strongholds everywhere but is split.
"Within the FLN there is a terrible conflict between reformists and conservatives. The FLN as such is definitely in danger but its ideas could be brought forward by other parties," the diplomat said.

FLN splinter factions -- including veterans of the 1954-62 independence war against France, and their children -- are already looking to form a Party for the Revolutionary Family, to take what they see as their legitimate role as those who won the war, in leading the country.
COALITION FORESEEN

Control Risks sees the same scenario: "Two political parties (FLN and Hamas) are best placed to attract most votes in the parliamentary elections scheduled to take place by the end of June 1997." No date has been set.

It suggests the Algerian military and Zeroual would prefer a Hamas-FLN coalition, perhaps with other minor parties, as this would limit the government's already highly circumscribed decision-making powers.
In 1991, diplomats said many of the voters who supported the FIS were disenchanted youths for whom the independence war was history. They were born afterwards.
Algerian officials see as a major challenge providing jobs, accommodation and hope for the under-30s who form about two-thirds of the population.
The budget for 1997 plans a housing levy to try to upgrade the crumbling capital Algiers, built for 750,000 people and now crammed with an estimated three to four million.
To provide work for about two million jobless -- 20 percent of the workforce -- Algeria is pumping money into industry outside the successful oil and gas sector.
Oil and gas exports, forecast at $12 billion this year and $16 billion in 2000, provide 95 percent of the foreign income.
Finance Minister Abdelkrim Harchaoui this month said he expected non-energy exports to double to $700 million within two years and hit $2 billion a year from the year 2000.
MORE FOREIGN VISITORS

Foreign perception of the risks of investing in Algeria has changed with visits by foreigners, including the French whose nationals formed the main group of some 100 foreigners killed in the North African country's conflict.
A European-based economic analyst, who also asked not to be named, pointed to encouraging signs of confidence.
"The reasons are that Algeria is seen to be very much on track with its International Monetary Fund restructuring programme and in good standing with the World Bank," he said.
"Hydrocarbons and foreign investment continue to improve and there have been -- albeit slow -- small steps politically."
